zurand

Overview

Random numbers in R come from a hidden, global state. set.seed() fixes where it starts, and every draw moves it on. So the numbers you get depend on everything drawn before: add one rnorm() early in a script and every later result changes, and split a loop across workers and the results depend on how the work was divided.

zurand has no hidden state. You make a key, and each value is worked out from the key and the value’s position, so the same key always gives the same numbers.

  • The same numbers everywhere. A key gives the same values on Linux, macOS and Windows, on Intel and ARM, and whatever the number of threads.
  • Nothing to keep track of. Drawing never changes anything, so drawing more, or drawing in a different order, leaves every other result alone.
  • Parallel work without worry. Give each task its own key, and the results no longer depend on how the tasks are scheduled.
  • Fast. Several times faster than runif() and rnorm() on one thread, and it uses more threads for large draws without changing a single value.
  • Huge vectors for free. A lazy vector of a billion values takes almost no memory: its values are computed only when you read them.

Installation

zurand is not on CRAN yet. Install the development version from GitHub:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zurand")

Usage 

library(zurand)

A key gives the same numbers every time you use it:

key <- rng_key(2026)
rng_normal(key, 3)
#> [1]  0.006686381 -1.233412249  0.591067060
rng_normal(key, 3)
#> [1]  0.006686381 -1.233412249  0.591067060

Asking for more values extends the sequence rather than changing it:

rng_normal(key, 5)
#> [1]  0.006686381 -1.233412249  0.591067060  0.835300390  0.249764157

For a simulation with several replicates, make one key per replicate. Each column holds the stream of one replicate:

keys <- rng_key(2026, n = 3)
rng_uniform(keys, 4)
#>            [,1]       [,2]      [,3]
#> [1,] 0.15037421 0.02841554 0.4769039
#> [2,] 0.91830293 0.65836513 0.1586149
#> [3,] 0.06342998 0.48395427 0.8484967
#> [4,] 0.74915105 0.79447021 0.9430020

Replicate 3 gets the same numbers whether or not replicates 1 and 2 ever run, on this machine or another:

rng_uniform(keys[3], 4)
#> [1] 0.4769039 0.1586149 0.8484967 0.9430020

When the parts of a computation have names rather than numbers, derive a key from the name:

rng_integer(rng_fold(key, "treatment"), 6, min = 1, max = 6)
#> [1] 6 3 5 6 4 3
rng_integer(rng_fold(key, "control"), 6, min = 1, max = 6)
#> [1] 6 6 6 3 5 5

A lazy vector is created instantly, whatever its length, and computes only the values you read. They are the same values rng_normal() gave above:

x <- rng_lazy_normal(key, 1e9)
length(x)
#> [1] 1000000000
x[c(1, 2, 3)]
#> [1]  0.006686381 -1.233412249  0.591067060

Every function is named rng_*(): rng_key() and rng_fold() make keys, and rng_uniform(), rng_normal(), rng_integer() and rng_bits() draw from them.

Acknowledgements

zurand builds on the Philox and Threefry generators of Random123 (Salmon, Moraes, Dror and Shaw, 2011), the xoshiro256++ generator of Blackman and Vigna (2021), the ziggurat method of Marsaglia and Tsang (2000) with NumPy’s tables, McFarland’s (2016) modified ziggurat, and fdlibm’s exp() and log1p(). The licences of the code it bundles are in inst/COPYRIGHTS. zurand itself is MIT licensed.
